She has vomited and is hard to keep awake.

sources.cite: NASEMSO. National Model EMS Clinical Guidelines, Version 3.0 (March 2022): Head Injury
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the full text Iowa HHS hosts (https://hhs.iowa.gov/media/198/download) through summarizing fetches with quotes; NASEMSO's own page, read the same day, still presents Version 3 (2022) as current and names no later version. Avoid hypoxia (no SpO2 below 90%) and hypotension; trend GCS or AVPU and reassess with any change in mentation; preferential transport to the highest level of care in the trauma system for GCS 3-13.

sources.cite: NASEMSO. National Model EMS Clinical Guidelines, Version 3.0 (March 2022): Patient Refusals
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 in the full text Iowa HHS hosts (https://hhs.iowa.gov/media/198/download) through summarizing fetches with quotes; NASEMSO's own page, read the same day, still presents Version 3 (2022) as current and names no later version. Capacity: 'alert, oriented, and can understand the circumstances surrounding his/her illness or impairment', judgment not significantly impaired by illness, injury or intoxication; a patient without capacity 'should not be allowed to refuse care against medical advice or to be released at the scene'; explain 'the possible risks and overall concerns'; doubts about capacity: contact medical direction; document the plan, who will be with the patient, and the patient's own words; tell them they may call again.

sources.cite: NHTSA. National EMS Scope of Practice Model 2019: Including Change Notices 1.0 and 2.0 (DOT HS 813 151, 2021-08-01)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17: the record page (title, report number, date; the change notices add intramuscular injection, vaccination in a public health emergency and nasal swab collection at EMT and above) and the PDF's skill tables through a summarizing fetch whose table columns were partly unclear, so placement was checked against the course's own reading (backend/supabase/seed/labs/ems-sources.ts, 2026-11-09) and REQ-241's reading (2026-11-11). EMR: oxygen, BVM, naloxone (intranasal or auto-injector), unit-dose hazmat antidote auto-injectors, tourniquet, wound packing, emergency moves, manual stabilization; no pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring or transport. EMT adds pulse oximetry, glucose monitoring, oral glucose, aspirin, the patient's own nitroglycerin, an inhaled bronchodilator, CPAP, the epinephrine auto-injector. AEMT adds IV and IO access, non-medicated IV fluids, supraglottic airways, waveform capnography, sublingual nitroglycerin and a limited list of IV and IM drugs (dextrose, naloxone). Paramedic adds 12-lead interpretation, manual defibrillation, synchronized cardioversion, transcutaneous pacing, needle chest decompression, intubation and medicated infusions. No newer model was found on 2026-11-17.
The objective and secondary objectives are the course's own titles.

The timing of her decline (drowsy and vomiting about 12 minutes after you reach her, as with a bleed under the skull on an anticoagulant) and the drive times are authored; FLAG: no source gives a rate. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

brief.situation: 14:20. You and your partner are EMTs on an ambulance, called by a daughter: her mother Ruth, 79, tripped on a rug about 40 minutes ago and hit her forehead on a table edge. Ruth is sitting up, talking, and says she is fine.
handover: The closest hospital is a community emergency department 8 minutes away with no neurosurgery; the regional trauma center is 25 minutes away.
Within EMT scope: assessment, pulse oximetry, glucose, oxygen, suction, positioning, transport and destination, and a refusal process with medical direction.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated seconds per real second. Pause any time.
Every assessment and treatment takes the time it would on a real call. Scene time and the drive run on the clock.
Partway through you are asked to explain your decisions in writing. The case ends when care is handed over, then a debrief scores what you did.

why.question: What in her history changed where she goes, and what will you watch for on the way?

parts.label: The history
parts.criteria: Age 65 or older with a significant head impact, and anticoagulant use (apixaban): field triage yellow criteria; a trauma center, not necessarily the highest level; she agreed once the risk was explained.
parts.modelAnswer: She is 79, hit her head hard and takes apixaban. Both are yellow criteria in the field triage guideline, so she goes to the trauma center even though she looks well.

parts.label: On the way
parts.criteria: Reassess GCS and vital signs at short intervals against the baseline; vomiting, drowsiness, rising blood pressure and slowing pulse are signs of a growing bleed; protect the airway (side, suction), notify the hospital.
parts.modelAnswer: GCS and vital signs every few minutes against her baseline of 15. Vomiting or drowsiness means a bleed may be growing: side and suction, and I tell the trauma center.

right.headline: The history changed everything
right.body: She looked well, but 79, a head strike and apixaban are yellow criteria: a trauma center. Reassessing caught the bleed growing, and the airway stayed clear.

leftHome.headline: A bump on a blood thinner
leftHome.body: She looked fine, but nobody asked about her medications or explained the risk before she signed. Ask about every medication, explain, involve medical direction.

aspirated.headline: Vomiting and drowsy: turn her
aspirated.body: A drowsy patient who vomits needs her side and suction within seconds.

scoring.modelReasoning: A 79-year-old who hit her head hard and takes apixaban meets two yellow criteria of the 2021 field triage guideline (age 65 or older with significant head impact; anticoagulant use), so she goes to a trauma center even though she looks well; ask about every medication to find this. Explain the risk; if she still refuses, involve medical direction. Reassess GCS and vital signs against her baseline; vomiting, drowsiness, rising pressure and a slowing pulse suggest a growing bleed: side, suction, notify the trauma center.

yellow.ask: While you take the history: which finding alone sends an alert, talking 79-year-old to a trauma center after a fall?

choices.label: She takes an anticoagulant and struck her head
Her age alone, with no head strike

yellow.explain: The 2021 field triage guideline lists anticoagulant use, and low-level falls in adults 65 or older with significant head impact, as yellow criteria: preferential transport to a trauma center.
